audit_trail_integrity.topic: Audit Trail Integrity and Tamper Evidence
audit_trail_integrity.conclusion_template: Audit trails must be append-only, cryptographically verifiable, and stored with tamper-evident controls. Every entry must include a timestamp, source engine ID, query ID, and SHA-256 hash chain. Gaps in the audit trail constitute a material control deficiency under AICPA AU-C 265 and must be reported to the Commander immediately.
audit_trail_integrity.reasoning_framework: Audit trail integrity is the foundation of all governance operations. Without reliable trails, anomaly detection becomes meaningless, compliance verification is impossible, and forensic replay produces unreliable results. The integrity framework requires: (1) Append-only storage — entries are never modified or deleted; (2) Cryptographic verification — each entry includes a hash that chains to the previous entry; (3) Timestamp validation — entries must have monotonically increasing timestamps within each engine; (4) Source authentication — engine IDs must match registered engines; (5) Completeness checks — gaps in entry_id sequences trigger alerts. NIST SP 800-92 establishes that log management infrastructure must ensure the integrity, confidentiality, and availability of log data. SOC 2 CC7.2 requires that the entity monitors system components for anomalies indicative of malicious acts. The audit trail is the primary evidence source for both requirements.
key_factors: Append-only storage mechanism prevents retroactive modification
SHA-256 hash chain provides tamper evidence across entries
Monotonic timestamp validation detects clock manipulation
Engine ID authentication prevents spoofed audit entries
Gap detection identifies missing or deleted entries
JSONL format enables streaming ingestion and line-level verification
primary_authority: NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management
AICPA AU-C 265: Communicating Internal Control Deficiencies
audit_trail_integrity.burden_holder: GOV02 Audit Controller — responsible for verifying trail integrity across all 507 engines
audit_trail_integrity.adversary_position: An adversary may argue that minor gaps in audit trails are inconsequential if other controls compensate. This position fails because audit trail completeness is itself a control, and gaps undermine the reliability of all dependent controls.
counter_arguments: Performance overhead of hash chaining is negligible (<1ms per entry)
Storage costs for full trails are justified by forensic value
Append-only prevents legitimate correction — mitigation: use correction entries, never modify originals
Clock drift across engines can cause ordering issues — mitigation: use UTC with NTP sync
High-volume engines may batch entries — mitigation: batch hash covers all entries in batch
audit_trail_integrity.resolution_strategy: Verify trail integrity on ingestion. Flag gaps immediately. Run periodic full-chain verification. Alert on any tamper evidence.
audit_trail_integrity.controlling_precedent: NIST SP 800-92 Section 4: Log Management Operational Processes

anomaly_detection_zscore.topic: Statistical Anomaly Detection Using Z-Score Analysis
anomaly_detection_zscore.conclusion_template: Query volume and latency anomalies are detected using z-score analysis with a threshold of 3.0 standard deviations from the rolling baseline. A z-score exceeding 3.0 indicates a statistically significant deviation that warrants investigation. Error rate anomalies use an absolute threshold of 15% as error rates do not follow normal distributions during incident conditions.
anomaly_detection_zscore.reasoning_framework: Statistical anomaly detection provides an objective, reproducible method for identifying unusual engine behavior. The z-score approach was selected because: (1) It adapts to each engine's individual baseline — a high-traffic engine naturally has different thresholds than a low-traffic one; (2) The 3.0 threshold corresponds to a 0.27% probability under normal distribution, providing high specificity (low false positive rate); (3) It requires no training data or ML models, maintaining determinism; (4) Rolling baselines adapt to gradual legitimate changes in traffic patterns. For error rates, absolute thresholds are preferred because error distributions are highly skewed — a single incident can produce burst errors that don't conform to Gaussian assumptions. The 15% threshold was calibrated against historical incident data from the ECHO PRIME fleet. COBIT 2019 MEA01.03 requires that monitoring thresholds be defined and calibrated to detect material deviations.
key_factors: Z-score threshold of 3.0 provides 99.73% specificity under normal distribution
Rolling baseline window adapts to natural traffic evolution
Separate thresholds for volume, latency, and error rate anomalies
Error rate uses absolute threshold (15%) due to non-Gaussian distribution
Minimum sample size of 10 prevents false positives on new engines
Severity escalation: z>5.0 = HIGH, z>3.0 = MEDIUM
primary_authority: COBIT 2019 MEA01.03: Monitor, Evaluate and Assess Performance
NIST SP 800-137: Information Security Continuous Monitoring
ISACA ITAF 2202: Risk Assessment in Planning
anomaly_detection_zscore.burden_holder: GOV02 Audit Controller — must maintain accurate baselines and detect deviations promptly
anomaly_detection_zscore.adversary_position: Statistical methods may generate false positives during legitimate traffic spikes (e.g., scheduled batch processing). Mitigation: known scheduled patterns should be excluded from baseline computation.
counter_arguments: Z-score assumes normal distribution — audit volumes may be multimodal
Rolling baselines can mask gradual degradation — mitigation: also track absolute thresholds
Minimum sample size of 10 may miss anomalies on rarely-used engines
Burst errors during incidents can skew baselines — mitigation: exclude anomalous periods from baseline
Time-of-day patterns may cause false positives — mitigation: compute baselines per time window
anomaly_detection_zscore.resolution_strategy: Compute per-engine baselines from last 1000 entries. Apply z-score threshold of 3.0 for volume/latency. Use 15% absolute threshold for error rate. Escalate severity based on z-score magnitude.
anomaly_detection_zscore.controlling_precedent: NIST SP 800-137: ISCM for Federal Information Systems and Organizations

tie20_compliance_verification.topic: TIE-20 Standard Compliance Verification for ECHO PRIME Engines
tie20_compliance_verification.conclusion_template: Every ECHO PRIME engine must implement all 20 TIE components to be classified as COMPLIANT. Engines scoring 90%+ (18/20 components) are COMPLIANT, 50-89% are PARTIAL, and below 50% are NON-COMPLIANT. Compliance is verified by analyzing the engine's /health endpoint response for evidence of each component. Non-compliant engines must be prioritized for upgrade within the next build cycle.
tie20_compliance_verification.reasoning_framework: The TIE-20 standard establishes a minimum viable architecture for production-grade intelligence engines. Each of the 20 components addresses a specific operational, security, or quality requirement. Missing components create specific risks: (1) No audit trail = no forensic capability; (2) No health endpoint = no fleet monitoring; (3) No determinism hash = no reproducibility; (4) No authority hardening = unreliable confidence levels; (5) No drift watcher = undetected doctrine degradation. Compliance verification uses a heuristic approach: the engine's health endpoint response is parsed for evidence of each component. This is a pragmatic approach because: (a) It requires no code access — only the health API; (b) It can be automated across all 507 engines; (c) It provides a consistent scoring methodology. The 90% threshold for COMPLIANT allows for engines that have legitimately omitted 1-2 components (e.g., vector_search on deterministic-only engines) while still maintaining high overall architecture quality.
key_factors: 20 mandatory components covering response, analysis, security, monitoring, and persistence
Health endpoint analysis provides non-invasive compliance checking
90% threshold allows for legitimate architectural exceptions
Compliance scores enable fleet-wide quality tracking over time
Non-compliant engines are prioritized in the build pipeline
Offline engines are automatically classified as NON-COMPLIANT
tie20_compliance_verification.burden_holder: GOV02 Audit Controller — must verify compliance for every engine in the fleet
tie20_compliance_verification.adversary_position: Some engines may argue that not all 20 components are relevant to their domain. While individual exceptions may be valid, the fleet-wide standard ensures interoperability and consistent monitoring capability.
counter_arguments: Health endpoint heuristics may produce false positives/negatives — mitigation: combine with code analysis
Some components may be implemented but not exposed in health response — mitigation: standardize health response format
90% threshold may be too lenient for critical engines — mitigation: per-tier thresholds
Offline engines may be intentionally shut down — mitigation: check registration status
Component quality varies even when present — mitigation: gate scores supplement presence checks
tie20_compliance_verification.resolution_strategy: Poll /health on each registered engine. Parse response for component evidence. Score and classify. Generate fleet-wide report. Prioritize non-compliant engines for remediation.
tie20_compliance_verification.controlling_precedent: ECHO PRIME TIE-20 Standard v1.0 — Mandatory Architecture Requirements

forensic_query_replay.topic: Forensic Query Replay and Audit Trail Reconstruction
forensic_query_replay.conclusion_template: Forensic query replay reconstructs the complete lifecycle of a query by assembling all audit entries sharing the same query_id, then correlating with temporally adjacent entries on the same engine. Reconstruction confidence is scored based on data completeness: full trails (query text + response + timing) yield >85% confidence, while partial trails yield proportionally lower confidence scores.
forensic_query_replay.reasoning_framework: Forensic replay is essential for incident investigation, compliance audits, and system debugging. The replay process follows a structured methodology: (1) Retrieve all entries matching the target query_id — this forms the primary audit chain; (2) Retrieve temporally adjacent entries (30-second window) from the same engine — these provide execution context; (3) Assemble a timeline showing the query lifecycle from receipt to response; (4) Score reconstruction confidence based on data completeness. The 30-second context window was selected because: (a) Most engine queries complete within 5 seconds; (b) Related queries (e.g., sub-queries, cache lookups) typically occur within 10 seconds; (c) 30 seconds provides margin for slow deep-analysis queries. Reconstruction confidence scoring ensures that consumers of forensic data understand the reliability of the reconstruction. A confidence below 50% should be flagged as requiring additional evidence from other sources (e.g., engine logs, network traces).
key_factors: Primary chain: all entries sharing the target query_id
Context window: 30 seconds before and after the primary entry
Timeline assembly provides chronological view of query lifecycle
Confidence scoring reflects data completeness
Max depth parameter prevents unbounded context expansion
Cross-engine correlation identifies distributed query patterns
primary_authority: NIST SP 800-86: Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques
ISO 27037:2012: Guidelines for Identification of Digital Evidence
forensic_query_replay.burden_holder: GOV02 Audit Controller — must provide reliable forensic capability for all fleet queries
forensic_query_replay.adversary_position: Forensic replay from audit trails alone may be incomplete — engine-side logs may contain additional detail not captured in audit entries. This is acknowledged in the confidence scoring system.
counter_arguments: Audit entries may lack query text for privacy reasons — reduces reconstruction quality
High-volume engines may have entry collisions in the 30s window — increases noise
Distributed queries spanning multiple engines require cross-engine correlation
Clock skew between engines may affect timeline accuracy
Deleted or expired entries create irrecoverable gaps
forensic_query_replay.resolution_strategy: Retrieve by query_id. Expand context window. Assemble timeline. Score confidence. Flag low-confidence reconstructions for supplementary investigation.
forensic_query_replay.entity_scope: Any query processed by any ECHO PRIME engine with audit trail enabled
forensic_query_replay.controlling_precedent: NIST SP 800-86: Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response

unauthorized_access_detection.topic: Detection and Response to Unauthorized Access Attempts
unauthorized_access_detection.conclusion_template: Unauthorized access attempts are detected by aggregating HTTP 403 responses and ACCESS_DENIED audit entries across all engines. Five or more denied requests from the same source within one hour triggers a MEDIUM severity alert. Twenty or more triggers HIGH. Fifty or more triggers CRITICAL and requires immediate Commander notification. Response includes source IP analysis, affected engine mapping, and temporal pattern identification.
unauthorized_access_detection.reasoning_framework: Unauthorized access detection is a critical security control for the ECHO PRIME fleet. The detection methodology combines: (1) Threshold-based alerting — fixed thresholds provide deterministic, predictable detection; (2) Source IP analysis — clustering denied requests by IP identifies targeted attacks vs. misconfiguration; (3) Engine mapping — identifying which engines are targeted reveals attacker intent; (4) Temporal patterns — burst vs. sustained attempts indicate different attack types. The tiered threshold approach (5/20/50) was calibrated to: (a) Avoid alerting on occasional legitimate authentication failures; (b) Detect persistent probing before it succeeds; (c) Escalate severity as risk increases. NIST SP 800-53 SI-4 requires information system monitoring to detect unauthorized access. SOC 2 CC6.1 requires logical access security to protect against unauthorized access.
key_factors: Tiered thresholds: 5=MEDIUM, 20=HIGH, 50=CRITICAL per source per hour
Source IP clustering identifies coordinated attacks
Engine targeting analysis reveals attacker objectives
Temporal pattern analysis distinguishes burst from sustained attacks
Cross-engine correlation detects fleet-wide scanning
Commander notification required at CRITICAL severity
primary_authority: NIST SP 800-53 SI-4: Information System Monitoring
NIST SP 800-61: Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
unauthorized_access_detection.burden_holder: GOV02 Audit Controller — must detect and alert on unauthorized access patterns across the fleet
unauthorized_access_detection.adversary_position: Threshold-based detection can be evaded by staying below thresholds (slow and low attacks). Mitigation: combine with behavioral analysis and long-term trending.
counter_arguments: Legitimate users may trigger 403s due to misconfigured permissions
Shared IP addresses (NAT/VPN) may produce false attribution
Threshold evasion via distributed low-rate probing from multiple IPs
API keys may be accidentally included in 403 logging — privacy risk
High threshold of 50 for CRITICAL may be too lenient for sensitive engines
unauthorized_access_detection.resolution_strategy: Aggregate ACCESS_DENIED entries. Cluster by source IP and engine. Apply tiered thresholds. Generate alerts with full context. Escalate CRITICAL to Commander.
unauthorized_access_detection.entity_scope: All ECHO PRIME engines with access control
unauthorized_access_detection.controlling_precedent: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SI-4: System Monitoring

soc2_trust_services.topic: SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria Mapping for Audit Controls
soc2_trust_services.conclusion_template: GOV02 maps to multiple SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria: CC6.1 (Logical Access Security) via unauthorized access detection, CC7.2 (System Monitoring) via anomaly detection and fleet health monitoring, CC7.3 (Detection of Unauthorized Activity) via access pattern analysis, and CC8.1 (Change Management) via drift detection. Each control mapping includes evidence collection procedures and testing methodology suitable for SOC 2 Type II examination.
soc2_trust_services.reasoning_framework: SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria provide the authoritative framework for evaluating the design and operating effectiveness of controls relevant to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy. GOV02's audit capabilities directly support multiple criteria: CC6.1 — Logical Access Security: The unauthorized access detection system continuously monitors for and alerts on unauthorized access attempts across all 507 engines. Evidence: ACCESS_DENIED entry aggregation, IP clustering, tiered alerting, Commander notifications. CC7.2 — System Monitoring: The anomaly detection system provides continuous monitoring of query volumes, latency, error rates, and health status. Evidence: Z-score analysis results, baseline computations, anomaly alerts. CC7.3 — Detection of Unauthorized Activity: Cross-engine correlation of access patterns enables detection of coordinated unauthorized activity. Evidence: Fleet-wide ACCESS_DENIED reports, temporal correlation analysis. CC8.1 — Change Management: The drift watcher monitors for unauthorized changes to engine doctrine configurations. Evidence: Drift event logs, version tracking, doctrine count monitoring.
key_factors: CC6.1 mapping: unauthorized access detection with tiered alerting
CC7.2 mapping: continuous anomaly detection across fleet
CC7.3 mapping: cross-engine unauthorized activity correlation
CC8.1 mapping: doctrine drift detection and version tracking
Evidence collection automated via audit trail and anomaly logs
Testing methodology defined for SOC 2 Type II examination readiness
primary_authority: AICPA TSP Section 100: Trust Services Criteria
soc2_trust_services.burden_holder: GOV02 Audit Controller — must demonstrate control effectiveness for SOC 2 examination
soc2_trust_services.adversary_position: SOC 2 compliance requires not just control existence but operating effectiveness over a period. GOV02 must demonstrate consistent, uninterrupted operation of its monitoring and detection capabilities.
counter_arguments: SOC 2 requires management assertion — GOV02 provides evidence but cannot self-assert
Control effectiveness requires period-of-time testing — point-in-time checks are insufficient
Auditor judgment may differ on control mapping completeness
Sub-service organization considerations may apply to engine-level controls
Complementary user entity controls may be required at the engine level
soc2_trust_services.resolution_strategy: Map each GOV02 capability to specific TSC criteria. Maintain continuous evidence collection. Generate period-of-time reports for examination. Support auditor inquiries with forensic replay.
soc2_trust_services.entity_scope: GOV02 Audit Controller and all monitored ECHO PRIME engines
soc2_trust_services.controlling_precedent: AICPA SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria (2017 Framework)

fleet_health_monitoring.topic: Fleet-Wide Engine Health Monitoring and Availability Tracking
fleet_health_monitoring.conclusion_template: Fleet health is monitored by aggregating per-engine health metrics from audit trail data and periodic health checks. Engines are classified as HEALTHY (error rate <10%, latency within baseline), DEGRADED (error rate 10-30% or latency >2x baseline), UNHEALTHY (error rate >30%), or OFFLINE (no response). Fleet-wide dashboards track uptime percentages, latency trends, and error rate distributions.
fleet_health_monitoring.reasoning_framework: Fleet health monitoring ensures that the ECHO PRIME system maintains acceptable service levels across all 507 engines. The monitoring approach uses audit trail data as the primary signal because: (1) It requires no additional instrumentation — audit data is already being collected; (2) It provides real-time metrics without polling overhead; (3) It captures the user-facing experience (latency, errors) rather than just infrastructure metrics. Health classification thresholds were calibrated against operational experience: HEALTHY represents normal operation suitable for production traffic; DEGRADED indicates the engine is functioning but below optimal performance; UNHEALTHY means the engine is producing unreliable results and should be taken offline; OFFLINE means no data is being received. Uptime tracking uses a time-series of health check results to compute availability percentages. This aligns with SLA requirements and provides historical trending for capacity planning.
key_factors: Health classification: HEALTHY, DEGRADED, UNHEALTHY, OFFLINE, UNKNOWN
Error rate thresholds: <10% healthy, 10-30% degraded, >30% unhealthy
Latency baseline comparison for performance degradation detection
Uptime percentage computed from health check time series
Fleet-wide aggregation provides system-level availability metrics
Per-engine reports enable targeted remediation
primary_authority: ISO 27001:2022 A.8.14: Redundancy of Information Processing
fleet_health_monitoring.burden_holder: GOV02 Audit Controller — must provide accurate fleet-wide health visibility
fleet_health_monitoring.adversary_position: Health monitoring based solely on audit trails may miss infrastructure-level issues (e.g., disk full, memory leak) that haven't yet affected query processing. Supplementary infrastructure monitoring is recommended.
counter_arguments: Audit-based monitoring has inherent lag — issues detected after impact
Engines with no traffic appear as UNKNOWN, not necessarily healthy
Health check polling may itself cause load on engines
Classification thresholds may need per-tier calibration
Fleet-wide averages can mask individual engine problems
fleet_health_monitoring.resolution_strategy: Aggregate audit data per engine. Classify health status. Track uptime over time. Generate fleet-wide reports. Alert on degradation patterns.
fleet_health_monitoring.controlling_precedent: ITIL v4 Service Level Management: Monitoring and Reporting

audit_report_generation.topic: Automated Audit Report Generation with Findings and Recommendations
audit_report_generation.conclusion_template: Audit reports are generated for daily, weekly, monthly, or custom time periods. Each report includes system-wide metrics (queries, errors, latency), detected anomalies, compliance status, top findings, and actionable recommendations. Reports are deterministically hashed (SHA-256) to ensure integrity and reproducibility. Findings are prioritized by severity and impact.
audit_report_generation.reasoning_framework: Automated report generation serves three critical functions: (1) Operational awareness — provides regular visibility into fleet health and performance; (2) Compliance evidence — generates documentation for SOC 2, ISO 27001, and internal audit requirements; (3) Trend analysis — enables identification of gradual degradation or improvement over time. Report content is structured to be actionable: findings describe what was observed, and recommendations prescribe specific remediation steps. The determinism hash ensures that the same input data always produces the same report content, enabling reproducibility for audit purposes. Report periods align with standard governance cadences: daily for operational review, weekly for management reporting, monthly for executive and compliance reporting. Custom periods support incident investigation and ad-hoc analysis.
key_factors: Configurable periods: daily, weekly, monthly, custom date range
System-wide metrics: queries, errors, latency, doctrine hit rate
Anomaly integration: detected anomalies included with severity
Compliance summary: fleet-wide TIE-20 compliance status
Findings: prioritized by severity with supporting data
Recommendations: actionable remediation steps
SHA-256 determinism hash for report integrity
primary_authority: GAO Government Auditing Standards (Yellow Book) Chapter 7
ISO 27001:2022 A.5.35: Independent Review of Information Security
COBIT 2019 MEA02: Managed System of Internal Control
audit_report_generation.burden_holder: GOV02 Audit Controller — must generate accurate, complete, and timely reports
audit_report_generation.adversary_position: Automated reports may lack the nuance of human-authored reports. However, automation ensures consistency, timeliness, and completeness that manual reporting cannot achieve at fleet scale.
counter_arguments: Automated findings may miss contextual nuances requiring human judgment
Report generation for large time ranges may be computationally expensive
Recommendations may not account for resource constraints or priorities
Determinism hash prevents report customization post-generation
Report recipients may need different levels of detail
audit_report_generation.resolution_strategy: Compute metrics for time range. Aggregate anomalies. Check compliance. Generate findings and recommendations. Hash for integrity. Deliver via API.
audit_report_generation.entity_scope: Fleet-wide or filtered to specific engine subsets

continuous_monitoring_framework.conclusion_template: GOV02 implements an Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) framework per NIST SP 800-137. The framework provides ongoing awareness of security posture, vulnerabilities, and threats through automated collection, correlation, and analysis of audit data from all 507 engines. Monitoring frequency varies by control type: access controls are monitored in real-time, configuration compliance weekly, and full security posture monthly.
continuous_monitoring_framework.reasoning_framework: ISCM transforms security from a periodic assessment to a continuous process. GOV02's implementation addresses the six ISCM steps: (1) Define — monitoring requirements are defined by TIE-20 standard and authority hierarchy; (2) Establish — baselines established per engine from historical audit data; (3) Implement — automated collection via /ingest endpoint; (4) Analyze — anomaly detection, compliance checking, and health monitoring; (5) Respond — severity-based alerting and escalation; (6) Review — periodic reports assess monitoring effectiveness. Real-time monitoring of access controls is essential because access violations have immediate security impact. Weekly configuration compliance checks balance thoroughness with operational overhead. Monthly full posture assessments provide comprehensive trending.
key_factors: NIST SP 800-137 six-step ISCM process implementation
Real-time access control monitoring via audit trail ingestion
Weekly TIE-20 compliance checking across all engines
Monthly comprehensive security posture assessment
Automated alerting with severity-based escalation
Historical trending for long-term security posture evolution
primary_authority: NIST SP 800-137: ISCM for Federal Information Systems
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CA-7 Continuous Monitoring
OMB M-14-03: Enhancing the Security of Federal Information
continuous_monitoring_framework.burden_holder: GOV02 Audit Controller — must implement and maintain the ISCM framework
continuous_monitoring_framework.adversary_position: Continuous monitoring generates large data volumes that may overwhelm analysis capabilities. GOV02 addresses this through statistical thresholds, baseline adaptation, and tiered alerting.
counter_arguments: Continuous monitoring requires continuous operational support
Data volume scaling challenges at 507-engine fleet size
Alert fatigue from false positives undermines monitoring effectiveness
Monitoring itself creates an attack surface (audit injection)
Framework maturity requires iterative refinement over multiple cycles
continuous_monitoring_framework.resolution_strategy: Implement six-step ISCM process. Calibrate monitoring frequencies by control type. Tune thresholds iteratively. Report on monitoring effectiveness.
continuous_monitoring_framework.controlling_precedent: NIST SP 800-137: Information Security Continuous Monitoring

error_rate_analysis.topic: System-Wide Error Rate Analysis and Root Cause Identification
error_rate_analysis.conclusion_template: Error rate analysis aggregates error entries across all engines to identify systemic failures, recurring error patterns, and root causes. Fleet-wide error rates exceeding 5% trigger WARNING findings; exceeding 10% triggers CRITICAL findings. Per-engine error rate analysis identifies the top error producers and correlates error patterns across engines to detect cascading failures.
error_rate_analysis.reasoning_framework: Error rate analysis is essential for maintaining system reliability. The analysis methodology uses three approaches: (1) Absolute rate analysis — computes error_count/total_queries per engine and fleet-wide to identify overall reliability; (2) Pattern analysis — clusters error messages to identify recurring issues amenable to GS343 auto-healing; (3) Correlation analysis — identifies temporal correlations between errors on different engines to detect cascading failures (e.g., a shared dependency failure). The 5% WARNING and 10% CRITICAL thresholds are industry-standard SRE benchmarks adapted for the ECHO PRIME context. Engines exceeding these thresholds are prioritized for investigation. Error message clustering uses substring matching to group similar errors, as full semantic clustering would violate the determinism requirement.
key_factors: Fleet-wide error rate computation with WARNING (5%) and CRITICAL (10%) thresholds
Per-engine error rate ranking identifies top error producers
Error message clustering groups recurring patterns
Temporal correlation detects cascading failures across engines
GS343 integration enables automated error healing for known patterns
Root cause categories: code bug, configuration, dependency, infrastructure, data
primary_authority: Google SRE Book: Chapter 4 — Service Level Objectives
NIST SP 800-184: Guide for Cybersecurity Event Recovery
error_rate_analysis.burden_holder: GOV02 Audit Controller — must track and report error rates across the fleet
error_rate_analysis.adversary_position: Error rate thresholds may be too aggressive for engines in development or testing. Mitigation: apply thresholds only to production-status engines.
counter_arguments: Error messages may contain sensitive information requiring sanitization
Clustering by substring may group unrelated errors with similar messages
Cascading failure detection requires temporal precision that audit trails may lack
Error rate fluctuations during deployment windows are expected
Not all errors are equal — severity weighting may be more appropriate than rate
error_rate_analysis.resolution_strategy: Aggregate errors by engine. Compute rates. Cluster messages. Detect correlations. Generate findings with root cause categories. Prioritize investigation by impact.
error_rate_analysis.controlling_precedent: Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives and Error Budgets

data_retention_policy.topic: Audit Data Retention and Lifecycle Management
data_retention_policy.conclusion_template: Audit data follows a tiered retention policy: hot storage (in-memory) retains the last 500,000 entries for real-time analysis; warm storage (JSONL on disk) retains 30 days of full audit trails; cold storage (R2 archive) retains 1 year of compressed audit data. Retention periods align with SOC 2 examination requirements and regulatory obligations. Data deletion follows secure erasure procedures.
data_retention_policy.reasoning_framework: Audit data retention must balance several competing requirements: (1) Forensic capability requires sufficient historical data for incident investigation; (2) Compliance requires retention periods aligned with examination and regulatory windows; (3) Performance requires limiting in-memory data to maintain query response times; (4) Cost requires archiving or deleting old data to manage storage expenses. The three-tier approach optimizes for all four factors: hot storage provides sub-millisecond access for real-time monitoring; warm storage provides second-level access for daily operations; cold storage provides minute-level access for historical investigations. SOC 2 Type II examinations typically cover 6-12 month periods, so the 1-year cold retention ensures full examination coverage. The 30-day warm retention covers typical operational and incident investigation windows.
key_factors: Hot tier: 500,000 entries in-memory for real-time analysis
Warm tier: 30-day JSONL retention on local disk
Cold tier: 1-year compressed archive in R2
SOC 2 examination coverage: minimum 12 months retained
Secure deletion: overwrite + verification for expired data
Lifecycle automation: tier transitions automated by age
primary_authority: NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management (Section 5)
data_retention_policy.burden_holder: GOV02 Audit Controller — must implement and enforce retention policy across all audit data
data_retention_policy.adversary_position: Longer retention provides more historical data but increases storage cost and privacy risk. The tiered approach provides a defensible balance.
counter_arguments: In-memory limit may cause data loss during high-volume periods
JSONL format is not optimized for complex queries — consider structured storage
R2 archive retrieval latency may be too slow for urgent investigations
Retention periods may not satisfy all jurisdictional requirements
Secure deletion verification adds operational complexity
data_retention_policy.resolution_strategy: Implement three-tier retention. Automate tier transitions. Verify secure deletion. Audit retention compliance periodically.
data_retention_policy.entity_scope: All audit data managed by GOV02
data_retention_policy.controlling_precedent: NIST SP 800-92 Section 5: Log Management Planning

authority_hardening_governance.topic: Authority Hierarchy and Source Conflict Resolution for Audit Standards
authority_hardening_governance.conclusion_template: Audit authority sources are weighted in a strict hierarchy: NIST SP 800-53 (0.95), SOC 2 TSC (0.93), ISO 27001 (0.92), COBIT 2019 (0.90), COSO ERM (0.88), IIA Standards (0.87), PCAOB AS (0.85), GAO Yellow Book (0.84), AICPA AU-C (0.82), Internal Policy (0.60). When authorities conflict, the higher-weighted source prevails. Internal policy never overrides external standards.
authority_hardening_governance.reasoning_framework: Authority hardening prevents the audit controller from producing conclusions that rely on weak or inappropriate authority sources. The hierarchy reflects: (1) Specificity to information systems security (NIST highest); (2) Broad industry acceptance (SOC 2, ISO); (3) Governance framework comprehensiveness (COBIT, COSO); (4) Professional standards relevance (IIA, PCAOB, GAO, AICPA); (5) Internal policy is lowest because it lacks external validation. The weight differential between tiers is calibrated to ensure that even partial matches with higher-authority sources outweigh strong matches with lower-authority sources. This prevents gaming through selective citation of convenient but weaker authorities. Conflict resolution is deterministic: when two authorities provide contradictory guidance, the higher-weighted authority's position is adopted as the primary conclusion, with the conflicting position noted as an alternative view.
key_factors: 10-tier authority hierarchy with explicit weights from 0.60 to 0.95
NIST SP 800-53 as highest authority for information security controls
SOC 2 TSC as primary audit-specific authority
Internal policy cannot override external standards
Deterministic conflict resolution by weight comparison
Weight differential prevents gaming through selective citation
primary_authority: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls
authority_hardening_governance.burden_holder: GOV02 Audit Controller — must apply authority hierarchy consistently in all analysis
authority_hardening_governance.adversary_position: Weighting authorities presupposes that higher-weighted sources are always more relevant. In practice, domain-specific standards (e.g., PCAOB for financial audits) may be more relevant than general security standards.
counter_arguments: Authority relevance depends on context — static weights may not capture this
New standards may not be reflected in the hierarchy immediately
Weight differences are subjective and could be debated
International variations may require different hierarchies
Internal policy may contain domain-specific requirements not in external standards
authority_hardening_governance.resolution_strategy: Apply weighted hierarchy to all authority citations. Resolve conflicts by weight. Note alternative positions. Review hierarchy annually.
authority_hardening_governance.entity_scope: All GOV02 audit analyses and reports
authority_hardening_governance.controlling_precedent: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems

confidence_stratification_audit.topic: Confidence Stratification for Audit Findings and Conclusions
confidence_stratification_audit.conclusion_template: All audit findings are stratified into four confidence levels: DEFENSIBLE (score >= 0.80, supported by strong authority and complete data), AGGRESSIVE (0.60-0.79, supportable but requires additional evidence), DISCLOSURE (0.40-0.59, material uncertainty requiring disclosure to stakeholders), HIGH_RISK (below 0.40, insufficient basis for reliable conclusion). Confidence is computed from doctrine hit, authority weight, anomaly count, and data completeness.
confidence_stratification_audit.reasoning_framework: Confidence stratification ensures that consumers of audit findings understand the reliability of each conclusion. The four-factor scoring model captures distinct aspects of reliability: (1) Doctrine hit (35% weight) — indicates whether the finding is supported by established audit reasoning; (2) Authority weight (30% weight) — reflects the strength of the underlying authority source; (3) Anomaly count (15% weight) — high anomaly counts suggest environmental instability that reduces confidence; (4) Data completeness (20% weight) — missing data directly reduces conclusion reliability. The threshold boundaries (0.80/0.60/0.40) create clear decision points: DEFENSIBLE findings can be relied upon for action; AGGRESSIVE findings should be corroborated; DISCLOSURE findings must be communicated with caveats; HIGH_RISK findings should not be acted upon without additional investigation.
key_factors: Four confidence levels: DEFENSIBLE, AGGRESSIVE, DISCLOSURE, HIGH_RISK
Four-factor scoring: doctrine hit, authority weight, anomaly count, data completeness
DEFENSIBLE >= 0.80: suitable for action without additional evidence
AGGRESSIVE 0.60-0.79: supportable with corroboration
DISCLOSURE 0.40-0.59: material uncertainty requiring stakeholder notification
HIGH_RISK < 0.40: insufficient for reliable conclusions
primary_authority: AICPA AU-C 700: Forming an Opinion and Reporting
ISA 200: Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor
confidence_stratification_audit.burden_holder: GOV02 Audit Controller — must stratify all findings and communicate uncertainty appropriately
confidence_stratification_audit.adversary_position: Four levels may be too coarse for nuanced audit situations. However, finer granularity risks false precision and inconsistent application.
counter_arguments: Weighting factors are subjective and may not suit all audit contexts
Anomaly count as confidence factor may penalize engines under attack
Data completeness measurement requires defining 'complete' for each query type
Stratification labels may be misinterpreted by non-audit consumers
Dynamic confidence (changing over time) is not captured by point-in-time scoring
confidence_stratification_audit.resolution_strategy: Compute four-factor score. Apply threshold boundaries. Attach confidence label to every finding. Include scoring rationale in DEFENSE mode responses.
confidence_stratification_audit.entity_scope: All GOV02 audit findings and query responses

zoned_analysis_separation.topic: Position Zone Separation in Audit Analysis
zoned_analysis_separation.conclusion_template: Audit analysis is conducted within strict zone boundaries: PLANNING zone addresses prospective questions (what should we do?), REPORTING zone addresses retrospective questions (what happened?), AUDIT zone addresses evaluative questions (is this compliant?). Zone boundaries must never be blurred — a REPORTING analysis must not include PLANNING recommendations unless explicitly requested. This separation preserves analytical independence and prevents bias contamination.
zoned_analysis_separation.reasoning_framework: Zone separation is fundamental to audit independence and objectivity. The three zones map to distinct analytical perspectives: PLANNING — Forward-looking, risk-based, advisory in nature. Answers questions about what actions to take, what controls to implement, or what changes to make. Uses projected data and scenario analysis. REPORTING — Backward-looking, factual, descriptive in nature. Answers questions about what occurred, what metrics show, and what the current state is. Uses historical data and observed facts. AUDIT — Evaluative, standards-based, judgmental in nature. Answers questions about compliance, effectiveness, and conformity. Uses criteria (standards) compared against conditions (observations). Blurring zones introduces bias: a PLANNING recommendation embedded in a REPORTING analysis can make reported facts appear to support a predetermined conclusion. An AUDIT finding embedded in PLANNING can constrain the solution space inappropriately.
key_factors: Three zones: PLANNING (prospective), REPORTING (retrospective), AUDIT (evaluative)
Zone boundaries are enforced at the query level
Cross-zone references must be explicit and labeled
REPORTING never includes recommendations unless explicitly requested
AUDIT uses criteria-vs-condition methodology
Zone separation preserves analytical independence
primary_authority: GAO Government Auditing Standards (Yellow Book) Chapter 3
zoned_analysis_separation.burden_holder: GOV02 Audit Controller — must enforce zone separation in all analyses and responses
zoned_analysis_separation.adversary_position: Strict zone separation may prevent holistic analysis where planning and audit perspectives are both needed. Mitigation: users can request multi-zone analysis with explicit zone labeling.
counter_arguments: Users may not understand zone distinctions and request inappropriately
Some queries naturally span zones and forced separation is artificial
Zone enforcement adds complexity to the response generation process
FAST mode may not have room for zone labeling in concise responses
Real-world audit engagements often blend advisory and assurance roles
zoned_analysis_separation.resolution_strategy: Classify each query into a zone. Generate response within zone boundaries. Label any cross-zone references explicitly. Default to AUDIT zone when unclear.
zoned_analysis_separation.entity_scope: All GOV02 query responses and analyses

determinism_verification.topic: SHA-256 Determinism Verification for Reproducible Audit Results
determinism_verification.conclusion_template: Every GOV02 response includes a SHA-256 determinism hash computed from the query, response content, mode, engine ID, and version. This hash enables verification that the same inputs produce the same outputs, which is essential for audit reproducibility. Hash verification supports forensic replay validation, regulatory examination reproducibility, and tamper detection.
determinism_verification.reasoning_framework: Determinism is a cornerstone of audit reliability. If the same query can produce different results at different times (without changes to the underlying data), the audit system's conclusions cannot be relied upon for compliance or forensic purposes. The SHA-256 hash captures the complete input-output pair for each query, enabling several use cases: (1) Forensic validation — when replaying a query, the hash can be compared to verify that the reconstruction matches the original; (2) Examination reproducibility — auditors can re-run queries and verify they get matching hashes; (3) Tamper detection — modified responses will produce different hashes, revealing manipulation. The hash includes the engine version because engine upgrades legitimately change response behavior. This prevents false tamper alerts during version transitions.
key_factors: SHA-256 hash computed from: query + response + mode + engine_id + version
Hash included in every query response
Enables forensic replay validation
Supports regulatory examination reproducibility
Detects response tampering or unauthorized modification
Version inclusion prevents false alerts during upgrades
primary_authority: ISO 27001:2022 A.8.1: Responsible Use of Assets
NIST SP 800-86: Forensic Techniques — Evidence Integrity
determinism_verification.burden_holder: GOV02 Audit Controller — must include determinism hash in every response
determinism_verification.adversary_position: Determinism may be impractical for queries involving external data sources that change over time. Mitigation: external data is snapshotted at query time and included in the hash computation.
counter_arguments: Hash computation adds latency (typically <1ms for SHA-256)
Non-deterministic components (timestamps, UUIDs) must be excluded from hash input
Engine upgrades legitimately change hashes — consumers must account for version
Hash alone cannot prove response correctness, only consistency
Hash storage increases audit trail size
determinism_verification.resolution_strategy: Compute SHA-256 on deterministic components of each response. Include hash in response and audit trail. Verify on forensic replay. Track hash mismatches as potential integrity events.
